subtype: Young person meeting a grandparent's forgetfulness [Observer]
passage:
Okay, Gurleen, you asked why I went quiet in the canteen. It's Nanaji. When I went home for Diwali, he called me Kamla, my mother's name, instead of Jaya. Twice. He asked if I'd eaten four times in one hour. And on Saturday he walked to the old market and couldn't find his way back. The shopkeeper phoned us.
I got really annoyed with him that evening. I said, "Nanaji, you just asked me that!" He looked so confused and small.
Then the doctor explained to us that this is an illness in his brain. He's not being careless. He can't help it.
Now when he asks if I've eaten, I just say, "Yes, Nanaji, rajma chawal," every time. He smiles. I still cry about it at night sometimes. But I'm gentler now.

qa.q: Who phoned the family when Nanaji got lost?
qa.a: The shopkeeper phoned them.

qa.q: What did Jaya feel when Nanaji called Jaya by the wrong name?
qa.a: Jaya felt confused and hurt, and later grief strong enough to cry at night.

qa.q: What helped Jaya respond more gently?
qa.a: Learning from the doctor that the forgetting is an illness, not carelessness, so Jaya now answers calmly every time.

qa.q: How might Nanaji have felt when Jaya snapped at him?
qa.a: He probably felt confused and ashamed, as he looked small after being told he had just asked.

grounding: It shows a student seeing a grandfather forget names, repeat questions and get lost, and responding gently after learning it is an illness.

subtype: Young person meeting a grandparent's forgetfulness [Observer]
passage:
My sister Chandrika came home from college for the holidays. I'm her younger brother, Tarun, so I notice things.
On the first day, Dadi asked Chandrika what she was studying. Chandrika said, "Economics, Dadi." Five minutes later Dadi asked again. Then again. By the fourth time, Chandrika's answer was short and she left the room. I heard her door close hard.
The next evening Papa sat us both down and told us Dadi's doctor had said the forgetting was an illness, not Dadi being careless. Chandrika didn't say much. I think she was upset, maybe with herself.
After that I saw her sit beside Dadi on the swing and answer, "Economics, Dadi," slowly and kindly, however many times Dadi asked. Once she even showed Dadi her textbook, and they laughed at the graphs.

qa.q: What does Chandrika study?
qa.a: She studies economics.

qa.q: How does Tarun think Chandrika felt after Papa's talk?
qa.a: Tarun thinks she was upset, maybe with herself, though he can't be sure because she didn't say much.

qa.q: What change in Chandrika's response could others learn from?
qa.a: She began answering Dadi slowly and kindly every time and even shared her textbook, instead of cutting the talk short.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel when Chandrika sits with her and shows the textbook?
qa.a: Dadi likely feels included and happy, since they laughed together at the graphs.

grounding: It shows, through a sibling's eyes, a student meeting a grandmother's repeated questions with impatience and then gentleness once she understands it is illness.

subtype: Young person meeting a grandparent's forgetfulness [Observer]
passage:
Friday: Gargi, twenty, came home from college and hugged Dadi. Dadi smiled politely. 'Which one are you, beta?' Gargi laughed awkwardly, then went to her room and cried. Later, when Dadi asked the same question about dinner five times, Gargi snapped, 'I told you already!'
Sunday: Her cousin Karthik, a nursing student, sat with her on the terrace. 'It's dementia. Her brain is changing. She isn't forgetting you on purpose.' Gargi felt ashamed of snapping.
The next Friday: When Dadi asked again, 'Which one are you?', Gargi took her hand. 'I'm Gargi, Dadi. Your Gargi who loves your pickle.' Dadi's face lit up. 'Ah, the pickle girl!' When the dinner question came again, Gargi just answered it, gently, each time.

qa.q: What did Dadi call Gargi on the next Friday?
qa.a: The pickle girl.

qa.q: What did Gargi feel when Dadi asked 'Which one are you?' the first time?
qa.a: She felt hurt and confused, laughing awkwardly and then crying in her room.

qa.q: What helped Gargi respond more gently?
qa.a: Understanding from Karthik that Dadi's forgetting was an illness, not carelessness.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel when Gargi snaps at her?
qa.a: Dadi may feel confused and upset without knowing why, since she does not remember asking.

grounding: Shows a young person meeting a grandparent's forgetfulness with grief and impatience, and learning it is illness so she can respond gently.

subtype: Young person meeting a grandparent's forgetfulness [Observer]
passage: Mohit, you're angry with Nanaji for asking the same thing again? Let your Baljeet Papa tell you something. When I was nineteen, my own grandfather, your great-grandfather, started forgetting. He'd ask me three times an hour if I'd eaten. Once he got lost walking home from the gurdwara, a road he'd walked for fifty years. I was so impatient. I used to roll my eyes, and once I shouted, 'You just asked me that!' He looked so frightened. I felt terrible. My mother told me, 'His memory is sick, like a sick heart. He isn't doing it to annoy you.' After that, I tried to just answer, kindly, every time. When he asked if I'd eaten, I'd say, 'Yes, Bauji, have you?' And we'd eat together. Those were good afternoons, in the end.

qa.q: Where did Baljeet's grandfather get lost walking home from?
qa.a: The gurdwara.

qa.q: How did young Baljeet feel after shouting at his grandfather?
qa.a: He felt terrible and guilty when he saw how frightened Bauji looked.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Baljeet's story?
qa.a: His mother explaining that Bauji's memory was sick, like a sick heart, so Baljeet began answering kindly.

qa.q: How might Bauji have felt when Baljeet answered 'Yes, Bauji, have you?'
qa.a: He probably felt cared for and included, and happy to eat together.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a young man impatient with a grandparent's forgetfulness who learns it is illness and responds gently.

subtype: Young person meeting a grandparent's forgetfulness [Observer]
passage: Ira, nineteen, had agreed to stay with Nana Jagdish for one evening while her parents went to a wedding. Then the power went out. In the dark, Nana got up and started walking towards the front door. 'I have to go to the office. They'll be waiting.' He had retired twenty years ago. 'Nana, there's no office. Sit down!' she said, too sharply. He turned, confused and frightened. 'Who are you? Where's my Kamla?' Ira's throat tightened. Nani had died years ago. She took a breath and remembered what her mother had said: it's the illness, not him. She lit a candle and spoke softly. 'Nana, it's Ira. It's night now. The office is closed. Shall we have tea?' He looked at her for a long time, then sat. 'Tea would be nice.' She held his hand until the lights came back.

qa.q: What did Ira light when the power went out?
qa.a: A candle.

qa.q: What did Ira feel when Nana asked for Kamla?
qa.a: She felt a tightening grief, since Nani had died years ago, and fear at his confusion.

qa.q: What helped Ira respond gently instead of sharply?
qa.a: Remembering it was the illness, not him, then speaking softly and redirecting him to tea.

qa.q: How might Nana have felt when Ira spoke sharply?
qa.a: He probably felt confused and frightened, not knowing who she was or why she was cross.

grounding: Shows a young person facing a grandparent's confusion with impatience and grief, and learning that it is illness so she can respond gently.

subtype: Young person meeting a grandparent's forgetfulness [Observer]
passage: Pankaj came home from his hostel in Nagpur for Diwali and found Dadi, Madhuri, at the gate with a shopping bag. "Where are you going, Dadi?" "To fetch Pankaj from school," she said, and looked right through him. His stomach dropped. At dinner she asked three times whether the sweets had come, and he snapped, "Dadi, I told you, yes!" Her face crumpled. Later, on the terrace, his mother explained that the doctor had called it dementia: Dadi's brain was changing, and she wasn't being careless. Pankaj sat with that for a long time. The next morning, when Dadi asked who he was, he said gently, "I'm Pankaj, Dadi. Your laddoo thief." She laughed, unsure, then patted his cheek.

qa.q: Where did Dadi say she was going?
qa.a: To fetch Pankaj from school.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when Dadi looked right through him?
qa.a: He felt shocked and hurt, a wave of grief and confusion as his stomach dropped.

qa.q: What helped Pankaj respond more gently the next morning?
qa.a: Learning that Dadi's forgetting was illness, not carelessness, so he answered calmly and playfully instead of snapping.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt when Pankaj snapped at dinner?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and confused, her face crumpling without knowing she had asked before.

grounding: Shows a student seeing a grandparent forget him and repeat questions, feeling grief, confusion and impatience, and learning it is illness so he can respond gently.
